articles.title: Fashion designer Henry Holland: ‘I’ve thought about a nose job but everyone says I’ll look different. That’s the point!’
articles.summary: Holland on his dashed Olympic dreams, ranking the Real Housewives shows, and a terrifying taxi ride. Born in Greater Manchester, Henry Holland, 43, worked as a stylist and fashion editor for Smash Hits magazine.
body: When were you happiest? In my late teen years, on that verge of having independence and no responsibilities.
What is your greatest fear? Going through grief and the loss of a parent was one of the toughest things I’ve ever done, so it happening again is my biggest fear.
What is your most treasured possession? This chain I wear round my neck, which was my mum’s.
What is your guiltiest pleasure? The Real Housewives – all franchises but primarily Salt Lake City, Beverly Hills and Orange County.
points: Holland on his dashed Olympic dreams, ranking the Real Housewives shows, and a terrifying taxi ride.

articles.title: Bailiffs and 100 unpaid teachers: inside the collapse of ‘groundbreaking’ yoga studio Triyoga
articles.summary: Formerly a favourite of the A-list, the chain has abruptly ceased trading, leaving teachers and customers blindsided. Kate Comer is a single mother with two children, so she is used to living on a financial knife-edge.
body: “I’m just reeling right now,” she said, estimating her loss at about £1,500. “I’m very concerned about the future.”

Comer is one of an estimated 100 yoga teachers who were not paid for their final weeks of teaching before Triyoga, the cult London yoga studio, shut. Several instructors of barre, spin and box-fit classes who taught at its sister brands Barrecore, Boom Cycle, Kobox and Reformcore, which have also closed, have also said they have been left out of pocket.
Yoga teachers who spoke to the Guardian said they felt blindsided by the sudden collapse, and are now struggling to pay essential bills. At least one says they are facing homelessness.

“It’s absolutely disgraceful and there’s nothing we can do about it as freelancers,” said Comer, who is currently going through a divorce and fears that her sudden loss of income will mean she is considered unable to keep the family flat. She is searching for other work, but “the market is saturated with hundreds of teachers”.

articles.title: In the footsteps of Wales’s heroic rebel prince: hiking Glyndŵr’s Way
articles.summary: As Michael Sheen prepares to bring Owain Glyndŵr to life on stage, our writer walks the peaceful national trail named after the last Welsh Prince of Wales. Between the treetops, I can see the towers of a distant mist-shrouded castle.
body: The towers slide away behind trees and a railway viaduct emerges. The medieval castle ruins, it turns out, are believed to have been plundered to build the viaduct in the 1860s, and the builders dropped in a couple of crenelated towers to honour the origins of the stone. I fear this may be an early omen: the spirit of Glyndŵr will be as elusive as the man himself was in his lifetime.

After his great rebellion of 1400 devolved into a murderous guerrilla campaign, the last Welsh prince of Wales simply disappeared. His English adversaries thought he had supernatural powers. Writing two centuries after the events, Shakespeare has Glyndŵr declare (under the anglicised name Owen Glendower) in Henry IV: Part I that “the earth did shake when I was born” and “I can call spirits from the vasty deep”. The last known sighting was in about 1819, when William Blake saw him in a vision and sketched his gaunt head. Since then, nothing. If he’s been hard to pin down for six centuries, what chance now?
points: As Michael Sheen prepares to bring Owain Glyndŵr to life on stage, our writer walks the peaceful national trail named after the last Welsh Prince of Wales.

articles.title: Tim Dowling: nobody’s laughing – is the joke on me?
articles.summary: By over-committing to the bit, I’m in danger of becoming the very thing that I mock. There was a kid in my year in high school named Jimmy Tremarelli. We were in a couple of the same classes, and also had occasion to pass each other in the hall between bells about three times a day.
body: Over the years the pretence became gradually more elaborate. Sometimes Jim would steal up alongside me at the end of class, cupping my elbow in the palm of his hand.
“Doctor,” he might say. “I know you’re busy, but I have a case I’d like to get your opinion on.” I would then stare at him gravely for a few seconds.
“Call my secretary,” I would say. Then we’d nod and go our separate ways. We were 15.

I can’t remember how or why it started, but in the hundreds of times Jim and I encountered one another over the course of three years, we never didn’t do it, not once. It wasn’t for anyone else’s benefit – I’m not sure anyone else even knew about it. I just remember students streaming round us, taking no notice as we stood there consulting in the corridor by the gym doors.
points: By over-committing to the bit, I’m in danger of becoming the very thing that I mock.

articles.title: Chicken Scarpariello
articles.summary: Crispy-skinned chicken thighs, sweet Italian sausage, and roasted potatoes meet a punchy, vinegary pan sauce.
body: Chicken scarpariello (shoemaker’s chicken) brings together crispy-skinned chicken thighs and Italian sausage in a punchy sweet-and-sour pan sauce. The Italian-American classic gets its tang from white wine vinegar and pickled Peppadew peppers, which mingle with onions, fresh bell pepper, garlic, rosemary, and all the savory drippings left behind by the meat.

While some chicken scarpariello recipes cook potatoes right in the pan, we roast fingerlings separately so they stay crisp—perfect for dragging through all that vinegary sauce. Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs are the move here: They brown beautifully, stay juicy as they braise, and add plenty of flavor to the sauce.

Peppadews add sweetness and a mild tang, but hot cherry peppers or pepperoncini work too if you want something sharper or spicier. Serve the scarpariello straight from the skillet for a hearty dinner that lands somewhere between weeknight comfort food and Sunday supper.
points: Crispy-skinned chicken thighs, sweet Italian sausage, and roasted potatoes meet a punchy, vinegary pan sauce.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Julian Klausner on Designing His Best Dries Van Noten Collection Yet
articles.summary: About 48 hours ago in Paris, Julian Klausner presented his spring 2027 Dries Van Noten ready-to-wear collection. For this Friday’s episode of “The Run-Through,” Nicole meets Klausner in the Vogue France offices to discuss the inspiration behind the show, his journey to Dries, and his industry peers.
body: “Yesterday, a friend of mine said that she saw it as ‘movie star meets picking up the kids,’” Kausner says, descibing the sensibility of the latest Dries collection. “I like to imagine what Marilyn Monroe would be looking like today if she had to run errands after a day of filming.”

Asked about the label’s ethos more broadly, Klausner says: “I think the playfulness and the invitation to be a little bit extra with your clothes is very much what we stand for.” He spends a lot of time in the archives, but he also sees Dries’s history walking around every day. “We have a lot of colleagues that have been there for decades,” he tells Nicole. “People are constantly wearing pieces from the ’90s or 2000s.”

Also on today’s episode: producer Chelsea Daniel catches up with Chloe for a quick fit check and to talk about the shows she’s attended since arriving in Paris; they speak to Jordan Roth after Schiaparelli; and we hear from the Chloé show’s hairstylist.
points: About 48 hours ago in Paris, Julian Klausner presented his spring 2027 Dries Van Noten ready-to-wear collection.

articles.title: Changing This Setting May Extend Your Battery Life on iOS 27
articles.summary: If you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you might have already put Siri AI to the test or tried out some of Apple's AI-powered photo editing features. But you may have also noticed something else: Your iPhone's battery isn't lasting as long between charges.
body: Technically, this feature isn't new. Before iOS 27, Apple called it "Wi-Fi Assist," but it worked a bit differently. In iOS 26, Wi-Fi Assist simply switches over to cellular when your wifi signal is too weak. With iOS 27's Connectivity Assist, it seems your iPhone can tap into both networks at the same time. If so, that may play some role in why this rejiggered feature seems to be dragging down people's batteries more than it used to.

There's another new addition with Connectivity Assist that could also be part of the problem: Unlike Wi-Fi Assist, Connectivity Assist sends DNS requests over cellular data, which can bypass the rules that ad blockers put in place to stop pop-ups from making their way into your iPhone. As such, even Apple recommends that you disable Connectivity Assist if you use an ad blocker. So, if your iPhone is constantly sending out DNS requests while on cellular data, bypassing your active ad blockers, that could be putting extra strain on your battery, too.
points: If you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you might have already put Siri AI to the test or tried out some of Apple's AI-powered photo editing features.

articles.title: Léa Seydoux on ‘The Unknown,’ Beauty, Fame, and Acting
articles.summary: Léa Seydoux talks Arthur Harari’s “The Unknown,” her approach to acting, and why she’s drawn to films about identity, mystery, and the unknowable.
body: Recently, Léa Seydoux was in a bathroom in New York when a woman—“very American, face full of makeup”—approached her with the nagging feeling that they had met before.
“I feel like I know you,” Seydoux remembers her saying, briefly slipping into a nasal American accent. “I’ve seen you somewhere.”

Seydoux, who has spent nearly two decades appearing in some of the world’s biggest films (including installments in the Mission: Impossible, James Bond, and Dune franchises), didn’t rush to solve the mystery for her. “I was like, ‘Really?’” she recalls, clearly amused by the encounter. After scrutinizing Seydoux’s face, the woman eventually decided that she simply reminded her of somebody she knew. “She couldn’t really place me.”

It’s an apt anecdote for Seydoux to relay while discussing The Unknown, Arthur Harari’s eerie, shape-shifting new film that premiered in May at Cannes, played at the Toronto International Film Festival last month, and is currently screening as part of the New York Film Festival.
points: Léa Seydoux talks Arthur Harari’s “The Unknown,” her approach to acting, and why she’s drawn to films about identity, mystery, and the unknowable.
